Mercury (planet) :: Orbit, rotation, and longitude :: Spin-orbit resonance :: chunk_0019
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/Mercury%27s_orbital_resonance.svg/250px-Mercury%27s_orbital_resonance.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Mercury%27s_orbital_resonance.svg)

After one orbit, Mercury has rotated 1.5 times, so after two complete orbits the same hemisphere is again illuminated.

For many years it was thought that Mercury was synchronously [tidally locked](/wiki/Tidally_locked "Tidally locked") with the Sun, [rotating](/wiki/Rotating "Rotating") once for each orbit and always keeping the same face directed towards the Sun, in the same way that the same side of the Moon always faces Earth. Radar observations in 1965 proved that the planet has a 3:2 spin-orbit resonance, rotating three times for every two revolutions around the Sun. The eccentricity of Mercury's orbit makes this resonance stable—at perihelion, when the solar tide is strongest, the Sun is nearly stationary in Mercury's sky.[[129]](#cite_note-131)

The 3:2 resonant tidal locking is stabilized by the variance of the tidal force along Mercury's eccentric orbit, acting on a permanent dipole component of Mercury's mass distribution.[[130]](#cite_note-Colombo-132) In a circular orbit there is no such variance, so the only resonance stabilized in such an orbit is at 1:1 (e.g., Earth–Moon), when the tidal force, stretching a body along the "center-body" line, exerts a torque that aligns the body's axis of least inertia (the "longest" axis, and the axis of the aforementioned dipole) to always point at the center. Guido Wilhelmus Imbens was born on 3 September 1963 in [Geldrop](/wiki/Geldrop "Geldrop"), the Netherlands.[[9]](#cite_note-9)[[10]](#cite_note-10) As a child, Imbens was an avid chess player.[[11]](#cite_note-11) In a 2021 interview, Imbens connected his passion for [econometrics](/wiki/Econometrics "Econometrics") to his childhood interest in the game.[[12]](#cite_note-12)

In high school Imbens was introduced to the work of Dutch economist [Jan Tinbergen](/wiki/Jan_Tinbergen "Jan Tinbergen"). Influenced by Tinbergen's work, Imbens chose to study econometrics at [Erasmus University Rotterdam](/wiki/Erasmus_University_Rotterdam "Erasmus University Rotterdam"), where Tinbergen had taught and established a program in econometrics.[[13]](#cite_note-13) Imbens graduated with a [Candidate's degree](/wiki/Candidate_(degree)#The_Netherlands_and_Belgium "Candidate (degree)") in Econometrics from Erasmus University Rotterdam in 1983. He subsequently obtained an [M.Sc.](/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree *[with distinction](/wiki/Latin_honors "Latin honors")* in Economics and Econometrics from the [University of Hull](/wiki/University_of_Hull "University of Hull") in [Kingston upon Hull](/wiki/Kingston_upon_Hull "Kingston upon Hull"), UK in 1986.[[1]](#cite_note-Imbens_Curriculum_Vitae-1)

In 1986, one of Imbens' mentors at the University of Hull, [Anthony Lancaster](/wiki/Tony_Lancaster "Tony Lancaster"), moved to [Brown University](/wiki/Brown_University "Brown University") in [Providence, Rhode Island](/wiki/Providence,_Rhode_Island "Providence, Rhode Island"). Imbens followed Lancaster to Brown to pursue further graduate and doctoral studies.[[14]](#cite_note-14) Imbens received an [A.M.](/wiki/Master_of_Arts "Master of Arts") and a [Ph.D.](/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy "Doctor of Philosophy") degree in economics from Brown in 1989 and 1991, respectively.[[15]](#cite_note-thesis-imbens-1991-15)[[1]](#cite_note-Imbens_Curriculum_Vitae-1)[[16]](#cite_note-16)
